---
title: "Step 1 · QC & host removal with VANISH"
subtitle: "Quality-control every read and make the human DNA vanish — before you count anything."
---

Before you count resistance genes, clean the reads. **VANISH** does two things in
one pass: it **quality-controls** every read (with `fastp`) and then makes the
host DNA **vanish** (with `bowtie2`). What comes out is quality-trimmed,
host-free FASTQ — ready for ResScan.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why bother stripping host DNA? Three reasons
**It's dead weight** — human reads carry no bacterial resistance genes and just cost
you mapping time.

**It protects your numbers** — tools that report AMR *per million sequenced reads*
(RPKM/FPKM-style) divide by your *whole* library, so human reads inflate the
denominator and can make a sample look artificially resistance-*poor* — sometimes
massively, and unevenly across samples with different host content. ResScan's default
**RPKPMC** is robust to this: it normalises *per bacterial cell* (via single-copy
bacterial genes), so human reads — which match neither the AMR genes nor those
bacterial markers — are simply ignored, and the estimate stays comparable. Robust,
not immune, though: heavy contamination still eats sequencing budget and sensitivity,
so strip it regardless.

**And it's the rule** — you must never archive human reads in public repositories
(privacy and consent), so **dehost before you deposit**.
:::

First, switch on the VANISH environment:

```bash
mamba activate vanish-env
```

## 1a · Prepare the read list

VANISH needs a small CSV pairing each sample's forward and reverse files.
`vanish-prep` builds it automatically — point it at the reads and tell it how the
mates are named (`_1` / `_2`):

```bash
vanish-prep --fastq_dir data/rawdata_10K --r1 "_1" --r2 "_2" --out read_pairs.csv
```

Have a look — one row per sample, forward and reverse:

```bash
head -3 read_pairs.csv
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
A ready-made copy also ships at `data/read_pairs.csv`, so you can skip this step if
you like — they're identical.
:::

## 1b · Run VANISH

Now dehost and QC all 36 samples. We point `--host_index` at the **toy** human
index that shipped with the repo, and keep `--cpus` modest for a laptop:

```bash
vanish --read_pairs read_pairs.csv \
       --fastq_dir data/rawdata_10K \
       --host_index data/host_index/toy_human \
       --cpus 4
```

On this 10K subset it finishes in a minute or two. You'll see Nextflow tick through
the three stages:

```default
 N E X T F L O W   ~  version 26.04.x
executor >  local

[..] FASTP_QC (SRR10842837)    [100%] 36 of 36 ✔
[..] REMOVE_HOST (SRR10842865) [100%] 36 of 36 ✔
[..] COMPILE_REPORT            [100%] 1 of 1  ✔

--- Vanish Run Complete ---
Status:   SUCCESS
Output:   vanished
```

## 1c · See what happened

The cleaned reads keep their original names, under `vanished/vanished_reads/`:

```bash
ls vanished/vanished_reads/ | head
```

And a per-sample report tells you what was trimmed and removed — reads in, QC
drops, host reads removed, reads out:

```bash
column -s, -t vanished/vanish_filtering_report.csv | head
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Expect almost no host removal here — that's by design
Our toy index is only the human *mitochondrion*, so it catches just a trickle of host
reads. The QC step is still doing real work. On real data with the **full human
index**, host removal is typically substantial — which is exactly why this step
matters.
:::

## Tidy up (optional)

Nextflow keeps a `work/` scratch directory that can balloon far beyond your input.
Once you've seen the results, reclaim the space:

```bash
rm -rf work .nextflow*
```

Finally, leave the VANISH environment before moving on:

```bash
mamba deactivate
```

Cleaned reads in hand — on to **Step 2**.
